meaning: 'Furrow' — the field-goddess, wife of Rāma and mother of his twin sons

pronunciation.approximation: SEE-taa — both vowels long, even and open.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit sītā carries two long vowels; the restoration Sītā keeps both macrons. Her name means "furrow" — the plough-line of the field from which she rose — making hers the rare theonym that is a farm word before it is a goddess, and the two macrons are the whole of its written dignity.

domains.title: The Daughter of the Furrow
domains.subtitle: Devotion, Exile, Trial, and the Opened Earth
domains.lead: Sītā is the epic of India told from its quiet center: the furrow-born princess whose abduction sets the Rāmāyaṇa in motion, whose fidelity survives fire, and whose final return is not to her husband but to the earth that bore her. She is virtue tested past every reasonable limit — and found whole.

cards.name: The Furrow
cards.desc: King Janaka found her in the plough-line of a sacrificial field — the earth's own child, named for the cut in the soil.

cards.name: The Fire
cards.desc: The agni-parīkṣā: the trial by fire she walked into to prove what everyone watching already knew.

cards.name: The Exile
cards.desc: Fourteen years in the forest, the abduction to Laṅkā, the second exile while pregnant — endurance as biography.

cards.name: The Return
cards.desc: Her answer to the second doubt: the earth opens, and the daughter of the furrow goes home.

symbols.name: The furrow
symbols.meaning: Her name and origin: the ploughed line — fertility, labor, and the earth's patience

symbols.name: The golden deer
symbols.meaning: The lure that crossed her threshold — desire engineered as trap

symbols.name: The fire
symbols.meaning: Proof demanded of the innocent; the trial that should never have been asked

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Her purity in every depiction from temple bronze to Madhubani painting

mythology.lead: The Rāmāyaṇa calls itself Rāma's story, but its moral engine is Sītā: every choice that matters is measured against her.

myths.title: Daughter of the Field
myths.text: King Janaka of Mithilā, ploughing a sacrificial field, struck something that was not stone: an infant in the furrow, whom he named Sītā — "furrow" — and raised as his daughter. Earth-born, not womb-born, the texts insist: her mother is the field itself, and the Rāmāyaṇa's most beloved heroine begins as a gift of agriculture. Her marriage to Rāma follows the bow of Śiva that only he could string.

myths.title: The Golden Deer
myths.text: In the forest of Daṇḍaka, during the fourteen-year exile, the demon Mārīca became a golden deer to draw Rāma from her side, and Rāvaṇa came as a wandering ascetic. She crossed the line — the lakṣmaṇa-rekhā drawn for her protection — only to give alms, and was carried through the sky to Laṅkā. A year in the Aśoka grove, under guard, refusing a king: the epic's center of gravity is her refusal.

myths.title: Agni-Parīkṣā
myths.text: Rescued after the war, she was met not with embrace but with doubt, publicly, before the armies. Sītā's answer was the fire: she walked into the flames, and Agni himself bore her out unburned, declaring her purity to the three worlds. The Rāmāyaṇa's hardest scene is also its most debated — every generation of India has argued whether the test was justice or injury, and the arguing is the point.

myths.title: The Earth Opens
myths.text: Years later, crowned and pregnant, she was exiled again on a rumor — and raised her twin sons in Vālmīki's hermitage. When Rāma finally came for her and asked one more public proof, she asked the earth instead: "If I have been faithful, open for me." The ground split, a golden throne rose, and the daughter of the furrow descended into the earth that bore her — the epic's most devastating line, and its most quoted.

lore.syncretism: Across Asia she travels with the epic: Thailand's Sida in the Ramakien, Cambodia's and Laos' Reamker versions, Indonesia's Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa, and the Jain tellings that soften the fire. In Nepal she is Janaki, daughter of Janakpur — the nation claims her birthplace and keeps her festival. The bhakti traditions make her inseparable from Rāma (Sītā-Rāma as one object of worship), and the Śākta readings make her the goddess herself in human trial: the earth-goddess borrowing a biography.
lore.culturalLegacy: Sītā is the standard by which Indian womanhood has been both honored and constrained — the "Sītā ideal" of fidelity and endurance, and the modern feminist re-reading that asks why the proving was hers to do. Her festivals (Sītānavamī, Vivāha Panchamī at Janakpur) draw millions; the Madhubani painting tradition of her Mithilā homeland depicts her in every home; Bollywood and television return to her constantly. Every debate on dignity, loyalty, and who owes whom proof in India runs, sooner or later, through the furrow.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sītā's story is the oldest case study in the difference between being good and being believed. She is proven right every time — by fire, by gods, by the earth itself — and the proving never stops being demanded. Her final answer is the only one that ends the asking: not another proof, but a refusal to be measured again. The furrow closes over her, and the field goes on feeding everyone — which is what the earth, all along, was trying to say.

lore.archaeology: Janakpur in Nepal's Terai keeps her city: the Janaki Mandir (1911, on older foundations) marks the site tradition calls her birthplace-home, and the Ram-Janaki Vivāha festival re-enacts the wedding annually. Mithilā's painted tradition (Madhubani/Maithil art, from the kohbar wedding-chamber murals) is among the world's oldest continuously practiced narrative arts. The Rāmāyaṇa sites across India and Sri Lanka — the Aśoka Vatika candidates near Nuwara Eliya, the Sītā Amman temple there — form the epic's living pilgrimage map.
lore.cult: Her worship began, fittingly, in a field. Late-Vedic house ritual already prescribes an offering to the plough's furrow — the halasīta-bali of the Gṛhyasūtra ritual literature — treating the cut in the soil as a goddess in her own right, and that furrow-goddess is Sītā's oldest layer. In the epics she is Rāma's wife and the daughter of the Earth; in living practice she is almost always worshipped beside him, as a single deity, Sītā-Rāma, whose image stands in home shrines and temple sanctuaries from Ayodhya to Janakpur. Her high days are the family festivals: Sītā Navamī in the spring month of Vaiśākha, and Vivāha Pañcamī at Mithilā and Janakpur, when the wedding is re-enacted before crowds that cross the Nepal–India border. The Ramlila cycles of the Gangetic towns stage her abduction, her fire, and her return each autumn. Her votive tradition is domestic: the kohbar wedding murals of her Mithilā homeland keep her on the walls of every bride's chamber — a cult painted rather than carved.
lore.iconography: The texts hand artists little: a woman of unmatched beauty, a lotus in her hand, the fire that would not burn her. From those few data the image traditions did their work. Her earliest monumental appearances travel with the epic itself: the ninth-century relief galleries of Prambanan in Java narrate the abduction and the war with Rāvaṇa in stone, and the twelfth-century builders of Angkor Wat cut her story into the temple's gallery walls. In India her image settled into the standing royal-couple type — Sītā at Rāma's left in bronze processional groups, crowned, her right hand raised in blessing — and the Pahari painters of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries gave her the intimate face the tradition still uses: the Kangra Rāmāyaṇa series shows her in the Aśoka grove, in the halo of the fire, on the throne. Ravi Varma's oleographs carried that Sītā into every bazaar at the turn of the twentieth century, and the Madhubani painters of her own Mithilā still paint her onto wedding-chamber walls today.
lore.reception: Sītā's journey is the journey of the book that carries her. Vālmīki's epic — scholarly datings run roughly from the mid-eighth to the mid-third century BCE — fixed her story; the Rāmopākhyāna of the Mahābhārata retold it inside the larger war; Kālidāsa's Raghuvaṃśa, fifth century CE, gave it the courtly version. The medieval vernacular poets then made her the property of every language: Kamban's Irāmāvatāram in Tamil, Krittivās in Bengali, and above all Tulsidas's Rāmcaritmānas (1574–77), whose Awadhi verses made Sītā-Rāma the household deity of northern India; the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa had already proclaimed her not heroine but goddess. Europe met the epic through eighteenth-century summaries and the first full translations at Serampore (Carey and Marshman, 1806–10) and in Griffith's Victorian verse (1859–75). The critical edition from Baroda (1960–75) and Goldman's Princeton translation (1984–2017) gave scholarship its modern footing, while the painted and performed traditions — Kangra albums, Ramlila stages, Mithilā murals — never stopped carrying her from one generation's eyes to the next.
